title: Harbor Retail microburst cost sensitivity brief
content:
Summary:
This doc captures the microburst/short-window load benchmarking we ran for Harbor (retail checkout assistant) to evaluate latency tail behaviour and incremental cost when adding burst capacity vs warming strategies. This is a working note for SE/Platform/Infra to decide an architecture for the POC (hosted vs dedicated hybrid).

Goal:
- Answer: for Harbor's expected traffic profile (90% small chat queries ~30-80 tokens, 10% long context product-explain ~400 tokens) how much does adding burst capacity (2x/4x spare GPUs) reduce p95/p99 during 1–5 minute microbursts and what is the incremental token cost per million for each strategy?
- Provide recommended config for POC (model variant, batching, cache strategy, fallback) with rough cost delta.

Test environment:
- Model variants: rwd-instruct-13b (fp16), rwd-instruct-13b-q4 (int8-like quant projection used in our runtime), and rwd-instruct-7b (fp16) as baseline.
- Hardware profiles: single A100-80GB pool (dedicated), H100-burst nodes (on-demand, dedicated), and hosted L4-like instances for cheap embeddings/short queries.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v2.5.3 with prefix-KV cache enabled, continuous batching on with batch_window=8ms and max_batch_tokens=2048.
- Traffic pattern: synthetic replay of production traces (April 2028) with microbursts modelled as 3-minute windows where QPS increases 6x over baseline. Baseline QPS = 12 qps, burst peak = 72 qps. Workload mix as above (90/10).
- Measurement slices: steady-state baseline (no bursts), cold-start bursts (idle cache + new session surges), warmed-cache bursts (cache preloaded with top-100 prefixes), and hybrid: dedicated pool + hosted overflow.

Procedure:
- Run each model/hardware combo 3x per slice, collect per-request latencies, GPU utilization, throughput, and per-route token cost.
- Calculate p50/p95/p99 and 95% CI across runs. Also capture tail CPU thread contention logs and runtime circuit-breaker events.

Key results (high level):
- rwd-instruct-13b (A100 pool, warmed cache, 2x dedicated capacity): p50=48ms, p95=210ms, p99=480ms at burst peak (72 qps). Token cost estimate: $85 / 1M output tokens.
- rwd-instruct-13b-q4 (A100 pool, warmed cache, 2x dedicated capacity): p50=42ms, p95=180ms, p99=420ms. Token cost estimate: $65 / 1M output tokens.
- rwd-instruct-7b (L4-hosted fallback for short queries, A100 for long): end-to-end P95 for short queries=95ms, long queries p95=520ms. Combined token cost approx $42 / 1M tokens (because most short queries on L4).
- Cold-start bursts (no cache): p95 increases by ~2.4x and p99 by ~3.8x across configs vs warmed-cache. Some spiky >2s p99s observed for long queries on fp16 13b when QPS>60 and no prewarmed KV.
- Dedicated extra capacity (4x spare GPUs) reduces p99 by ~28% compared to 2x spare; but incremental monthly cost is non-linear (2.8x cost vs 2x capacity).

Observations / notes:
- Quantized variant (q4) shows consistent latency improvement and ~23% lower GPU utilization for same throughput; quality regression checks (small eval set) show negligible BLEU-style differences for Harbor prompts, but need product QA.
- The majority of observed tail (p99) comes from long-context responses hitting kernel-level memory pressure and runtime GC spikes when KV cache entries exceed warm-target.
- Overflow to hosted L4 for short queries is effective: reduces token-weighted p95 by ~35% while lowering cost. But adds routing complexity (two-model routing, increased op-exposure).
- Autoscaling reaction time matters: default cooldown/scale-up latency (~90s) is too slow for 3-minute microbursts. Either provisioned burst capacity or predictive warmers required.

Detailed numbers (selected):
- A100, rwd-13b-q4, warmed-cache, 2x capacity, burst peak 72 qps:
  - p50=42ms, p75=85ms, p95=180ms, p99=420ms. GPU util avg=68%, burst-period GC events=2 per node.
- A100, rwd-13b fp16, cold-start burst:
  - p50=140ms, p95=510ms, p99=1250ms. Several >2s tails correlated with disk-swap activity on one node (investigate run #2 logs).
- Hybrid routing (7b for short, 13b for long) overall throughput handled peak with no >1.2s tail for short queries; long queries still contributed most absolute tokens and cost.

Cost sensitivity (ballpark monthly assumptions for POC):
- Baseline (2x capacity, no overflow): $18k/mo (dedicated A100 pool) + $4k/mo infra = $22k/mo.
- Add hosted overflow (L4) and predictive warmers: $22k + $3.5k = $25.5k/mo but 37% lower expected token cost at peak because short queries charged cheaper hosted token rate.
- 4x reserved capacity jumps to $47k/mo (non-linear because of instance classes) — reduces p99 but not cost-efficient for short bursts under 5 minutes.

Anomalies / run-specific notes:
- Run 2028-04-22_14:03 (A100 fp16 cold burst): one node reported OOM-reallocation and a kernel fallback to slower path for ~14s, producing a 9s outlier. Ticketed as RW-OPS-331.
- Warmed-cache runs show a small steady-state error increase in some productExplain prompts; hypothesis: q4 quantized weights slightly shift tokenization logits for rare tokens. Action: add token-level regression tests.

Recommendations for Harbor POC (vote):
1) Use hybrid routing: route short queries (<100 tokens) to cheaper hosted L4 pool; route long-context (>=100 tokens) to dedicated A100 with rwd-instruct-13b-q4. This balances cost and tail.
2) Provision 2x dedicated capacity for steady load + a predictive warm-up job that preloads top-200 prefixes 90s before expected promo bursts (based on traffic signal).
3) Implement circuit-breaker policy for long queries: degrade to 7b fallback when p95 crosses healthy threshold; surface quality alerts to Product.
4) For 3-month POC, budget for hosted overflow + warming strategy instead of 4x dedicated GPUs — better cost/benefit for 1–5 minute microbursts.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Product signoff: is an occasional fallback to 7b acceptable for UX? (Renee to confirm).
- Add automated regression eval for token-level diffs between fp16 and q4 on Harbor canonical prompts (Marco owner).
- Validate AWS pricing delta with Finance for the months with promotional traffic spikes (Benji).
- Investigate OOM event in RW-OPS-331 and whether kernel fallback is reproducible on H100 nodes.

Next steps:
- Prep a one-page POC proposal for GTM/Customer that lists recommended architecture and estimated monthly P&L (deliver by 2028-05-07).
- Create a lightweight demo showing routing behavior (short->L4, long->13b-q4) and dashboard that surfaces p95 per-route.
- Schedule cross-team run to reproduce OOM (ops+runtime) and add guardrails to runtime release checklist.

Notes to self / rough items:
- Keep track of RW-6789 (Harbor feature epic) and attach final numeric table.
- Slack thread: #harbor-poc contains raw CSVs from runs (link above).
- This doc is intentionally informally structured; will produce final slide with 3 recommendation options after we get product feedback.

-- Aisha
